The present appeal was preferred by the appellant on 24.04.2014 and was assigned to the then learned ASJ/FSSA Court and after administrative directions vide order no. 12072-12106/ Judl.
/NDD/PHC/ND dated 01.10.2019 it was assigned to this court for disposal of the same as per law.

2. By way of present appeal, the appellant herein has challenged the judgment dated 21.03.2014 and order on the point of sentence dated 24.03.2014 passed by the then learned ACMM-II, PHC, New Delhi vide which the appellant/accused was held guilty for commission of offences punishable under sections 16(1A) r/w Section 7 of PFA Act, 1954, the appellant was awarded a sentence to undergo Simple Imprisonment for 18 months as well as to pay fine of Rs. 10,000/- for commission of aforesaid offences and in dafault of payment of fine to undergo Simple Imprisonment of 60 days.
Benefit of Section 428 Cr.P.C, if any, applicable was given to him.

- that the complaint was filed in writing by a public servant, hence, recording of pre-summoning evidence was dispensed with ;
4.

The appellant/accused Pankaj Aggarwal being the Vendor cum Proprietor and Sh. Mahavir Prasad as Licencee of the said shop/business premises were summoned by the learned trial court vide order dated 28.03.2006 for 08.04.2006 to face trial.
Thereafter the accused persons appeared to face trial but during the trial proceedings Sh. Mahavir Prasad expired on 19.10.2007 and proceedings against him were abated vide order dated 18.11.2008.

sentences.text: Thereafter matter was listed for pre-charge evidence, wherein the complainant examined PW-1 Sh.Suniti Kumar Gupta, Food Inspector.

6. On the basis of testimony of prosecution witnesses on 22.12.2009 charge was framed against the appellant/accused for commission of offences punishable u/s 7/16(1A) of PFA Act for violation of provisions of Sub clause 2(ia)(j)and(m) of PFA Act alleging therein that on 26.10.2005 at about 08.15 p.m, appellant/accused being the the Vendor cum Proprietor of M/s Aggarwal Sweets sold for analysis approximately 1500 grams of "Imli Ki Chatni" taken from an open tin bearing no label declaration to Food Inspector Sh.Suniti Kumar Gupta on payment of sample commodity in the presence of LHA and witnesses and it was analyzed by the PA vide Certificate No.
PFA/Enf./2590/2005 on 07.11.2005 and found that the sample is adulterated because it is coloured with synthetic colouring material viz sunset yellow FCF and violated the provisions of Section 2(ia)(a)(j) & (m) of PFA Act, 1954 and also violated the provision of Rule 23 read with Rule 28 & 29 of PFA Rules, 1955, punishable under section 16(1A) of PFA Act, 1954 to which he pleaded not guilty and claimed trial.

6.1 During trial after the examination and detailed cross examination of three witnesses of the department ( PW-1 Sh.Suniti Kumar Gupta, Food Inspector, PW-2 Sh.Satish Kumar Gaur, Field Assistant and PW-3 Sh. Vijay Dogra, Retired Jail Supdt, the then SDM/LHA prosecution evidence was closed and matter was fixed for Statement of accused.

7. The statement of appellant/accused was recorded under section 313 Cr.PC in which he pleaded his innocence and stated that no efforts were made to join the public witnesses, the Imli Ki Chatni was lying in a plastic container ; that the container was not bearing label or declaration ; that the spoon used for taking sample was not dry and clean ; no payment was made as the commodity was not for sale ; consent was granted without application of mind, it is a false case and he has been falsely implicated.
He prefer to lead defence evidence however, no witness was produced or examined as a defence witness.

7.1 After hearing the arguments of both the parties, appellant was convicted by the learned trial court for commission of offence punishable u/s 7/16(1)(a) PFA Act for violation of Section 2(ia)(a)
(j)&(m) of PFA Act, 1954 read with Rules 23,28 and 29 of PFA Rules .

8. The learned trial court in its impugned judgment dated 21.03.2014 observed that the samples had been collected according to the prescribed procedures from the vendor cum Proprietor/ appellants premises, on analyzing the sample, it was opined by the PA vide Certificate No.
PFA/Enf./2590/2005 on 07.11.2005 and found vide his report that the sample is adulterated because it is coloured with synthetic colouring material viz sunset yellow FCF.

The appellant was accordingly convicted and sentenced by the learned trial court and aggrieved by the said judgment and order on quantum of sentence dated 24.03.2014, the present appeal has been preferred by the appellant.
9.(I) The appellant has assailed the judgment and order on sentence passed by the learned trial court by urging various grounds.

sentences.text: Alternatively, on the quantum of sentence, relying upon the new legislation, it was pleaded that the case of the appellant be considered sympathetically in the light of the preposition of law laid down by the Hon'ble Courts pursuant to coming of new legislation that is Food Safety & Standards Act.

10. During the course of argument on 18.03.2021, learned counsel for the appellant submitted that appellant is not challenging the merits of the case/ conviction decided by the learned trial court vide judgment dated 21.03.2014, and is confining his appeal limited to the quantum of sentence only awarded to him vide order dated 24.03.2014 ; and to affirm his submissions, appellant has tender his affidavit duly sworn and notarized by the Oath Commissioner, in that regard and prayed that a lenient view be taken against him by giving him the benefit of New Legislation as FSSAI.
11.

Learned counsel for the Delhi Admn./Food Department, objected to the same and submitted that according to submission of appellant, prosecution has established its case and he be sentenced with strict punishment in terms of old Act wherein minimum punishment is prescribed and no leniency should be shown to the convict as it is a serious offence of food adulteration article / commodity leading to hazardous consequences on the health or body of a person.
12. I have carefully gone through the available record as well as trial court record, have heard the submissions of learned counsel for both the parties at length and have also gone through the judgments relied upon by the parties.
13. In light of above submissions and discussion particularly when the affidavit of appellant to this effect is filed on record, I find no valid and legal reasons to interfere with the well reasoned judgment of the learned trial court.
The findings of the learned trial court with respect to the conviction of the appellant for the offence punishable under 16(1A) of the PFA Act read with Section 7 of the PFA Act, 1954 are upheld.
II. Now Coming to the alternate plea of giving benefit of new legislation to the appellant/ accused.
14. It is argued by learned counsel for the appellant that on the date of pronouncement of judgment/order on sentence, the PFA Act, 1954 was repealed and new act has thereafter come into operation.

It is stated that the court should give benefit of the new legislation to the accused vide which the punishment provided under the old act has been diluted to a considerable extent, and that the offence for which the accused/appellant has been convicted now falls under the category of "Unsafe Food" punishable under section 59(1) of the new Act i.e Food and Safety Standards Act,
2006 (hereinafter called FSSAI) punishable upto six months and fine of upto Rs. One lac only.
15.

It was argued by learned counsel for the appellant that appellant is a man of 38 years of age,
respectable person, has deep roots in the society and only sole bread earner of his family, the licencee of the M/s Aggarwal Sweets was his father, (accused no. 2 before the trial court ) has expired, and his mother is a paralytic patient, totally dependent upon him, is still running the same business at the same place, not involved into any offence under the PFA Act and there is no case subsequent thereto till date, and thus, prayed that a lenient view be taken against him in the light of Pankaj Aggarwal vs The State ( Govt Of Nct Of Delhi) on 18 March, 2021 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/107673412/
4 the provisions of law under the new Act.

entities.text: Pankaj Aggarwal vs The State ( Govt Of Nct Of Delhi)
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: 15.1 Further it is stated that case pertains to the year 2006, the appellant/accused has faced the trial almost 15 years which by itself is a sufficient punishment and, the hardships faced by him has caused him great mental agony, stress and rigors of trial during the said period.

It is also stated that now a days special circumstances exists due to outbreak of pandemic of Covid-19 and there are chances of appellant being infected with virus in case imprisonment of sentence is awarded to him.

15.2 In support of his submissions qua the consideration of the case under new legislation, learned counsel for appellant had relied upon the judgment of Nemi Chand Vs. State of Rajasthan ( Crl.
Appeals No. 214 and 215 of 2016, vide order dated 10.03.2016, as corrected vide order dated 17.03.2016, as reported in 2016 (1) FAC 203 ) of Hon'ble Supreme Court and earlier judgment T Barai Vs. Henry 1983 ( ) SCC 177.
15.3

entities.text:
Nemi Chand Vs. State of Rajasthan ( Crl.
Appeals No. 214 and 215 of 2016
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Per contra, learned SPP, strongly opposed the submissions advanced by learned counsel by addressing that the sentencing cannot be done in new Act since the definition of many offences have changed in the new Act including this particular offence of which accused is charged.
Definition of major offences like "adulteration" and "misbranding" have been changed.
Now FSSAI have definition "substandard food", "food containing extraneous matter" "unsafe food" and misbranded food".
Due to this reason, the ingredients have changed and thus there is no way in which the old offences could be related to new offences.
15.4 In the present case, the offence was that the food article i.e. Imli Ki Chutni was found adulterated and was unfit for human consumption.
This was violation of Section 2(ia)(a) (j)&(m) of PFA Act, 1954 read with Rules 23,28 and 29 of PFA Rules, punishable under section 16(1A) of PFA Act, 1954.
15.5 That now in the FSSAI such adulteration is termed as "unsafe food" in terms of Section 3(zz)(viii) of FSSA Act and violation thereof is punishable u/s 59(1) of FSSA.
So if we go through both these provisions of law a particular offence with a particular fact is mentioned with some other name but with same ingredients in the New FSSA Act.

- Sub-clause (viii) of 3(zz) FSSA Act is applicable where the colouring material or the preservative other than that specified in respect there of is found in the food article and not where the colouring material exceeds the prescribed limit.
15.6 Further, the charge in this case was framed for the said offences and there is no charge in which it is stated that the said adulteration was injuries to health.

Had it been the case, the charge would have been for the offence punishable u/s 16(1-A)(ii) of PFA Act r/w section 2(ia)(l) & (f).
15.7
Thus, it is held that it is the ingredients which constitute an offence and determines whether it is the same offence but with new name or an altogether different offence,

Here the offence of adding colour in the food article which was punishable u/s 16(1)(a) PFA Act is similar to the offence u/s 59 of FSSAI Act, which is now punishable with simple imprisonment of six months and fine upto one lakh.

sentences.text: Now, coming to the application of Nemi Chand Judgment (supra), the same is based on the old judgment i.e. T Barai ( Supra) of Hon'ble Supreme Court.

The relevant portion of the T Barai Judgment is as follows :
- (Para 25) It is settled both on authority and principle that when a later statute again describes an offence created by an earlier statute and imposes a different punishment or varies the procedure, the earlier statute is repealed by implication in Michell Vs.
Brown ( 1958) 120 ER 909, 912 : 32 LTOS 146:7 WR 80 Lord Campbell put the matter thus :
- "It is well settled rule of construction that, if a later statute again describes an offence created by a former statute and affixes a different punishment, varying the procedure, the earlier statute is repealed by the later statute see also Smith Vs.
Benabo ( 1937) 1 ALL ER 523 : ( 1997) 1 KB 518: 156 LT 194"

entities.text:
Michell Vs.
Brown ( 1958) 120 ER 909, 912 : 32 LTOS 146:7 WR 80
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
- In Regina Vs. Youle ( 1861) 158 ER 311,315-16 : LT 299 : 9 WR 637 Martin B. said in the oft-quoted passage :
- If a statute deals with a particular class of offences, and a subsequent Act is passed which deals with precisely the same offence, and a different punishment is imposed by the later Act, I think that, in effect, the legislature has declared that the new Act shall be substituted for the earlier Act."
- The rule is however subject to the limitation contained in Article 20(1) against ex post facto law providing for a greater punishment and has also no application where the offence described in the later Act is not the same as in the earlier Act i.e. when the essential ingredients of the two offences are different.
- Moreover, this particular aspect is stated as a illustration in the same judgment in Para 23 which is as follows :
- To illustrate, if Parliament were to reenact Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code,
1860 and provide that the punishment for an offence of murder shall be sentence for imprisonment for life instead of the present sentence of death or imprisonment for life, then it can not be that the courts would still award a sentence of death even in pending cases.
15-A - Academic Reference can also be made to the letter dated 03.10.2017 of Food Safety and Standards Authority of India, produced before the court during the proceedings.

entities.text: Food Safety and Standards Authority of India
entities.label: ORG

sentences.text: Vide said letter the said authority, in the light of judgment of Hon'ble Supreme Court in Nemi Chand's Case (supra) issued an advisory to the Commissioners of Food Safety/Officers incharge of Food Safety to dispose of the long pending court cases filed under old PFA Act mainly concerning substandard and misbranding by imposing fine only.

6 15-B -

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: In view of the above mentioned discussion, it can be safely said that while considering the point of sentence, in backdrop of the object and reasons of the act and the intention of the legislature, the quantum of sentence so passed in the interest of justice needs to be considered under the new Act i.e. FSSAI, while deciding the present appeal.

16. Thus, analyzing the facts of the case, taking note of the special circumstances of the case and the fact that accused has faced the trial of almost 15 years ; in light of the above cited judgment and the judgment of Hon'ble High Court of Delhi titled as GNCT Vs. Jagdish Tyagi dated 11.10.2017 in my view the convict/ appellant is entitled to the benefit of new legislation.

Accordingly to meet the ends of justice, the sentence of the convict Pankaj Aggarwal as imposed by the learned trial court vide order dated 24.03.2014 stands modified to the extent that the order sentencing the appellant to undergo simple imprisonment of 18 months stands waived off to simple imprisonment for one day i.e. till rising of the court ; the sentence of fine is enhanced from Rs. 10,000/- to Rs. 1,00,000/-
In default of payment of fine the appellant/convict shall undergo simple imprisonment for two months.
Sentence modified accordingly.

17 Appellant/Convict is directed to deposit the fine amount within 8 weeks from the date of pronouncement of this judgment before the learned trial court and, if any, amount of fine was deposited by the appellant before the learned trial court same shall be adjusted accordingly.
18. The present appeal is disposed of accordingly in terms thereof.
19. TCR be sent back with alongwith copy of the judgment to the learned trial court.
20. Appeal file be consigned to record room after completion of all other necessary formalities.
